presentingComplaint: New, severe left-sided headache for 3 weeks with pain in the jaw on chewing.
history: 72-year-old woman presents with a 3-week history of a new-onset, persistent, throbbing left temporal headache, unlike any headache she has had before. She reports scalp tenderness (combing her hair is painful) and jaw claudication - aching in the jaw muscles after a few minutes of chewing that resolves with rest. Over the same period she has had low-grade fevers, drenching night sweats, and unintentional weight loss of about 3 kg. She denies visual loss, diplopia, or transient visual obscurations, but admits to occasional blurring that resolves quickly. No history of trauma, sinus symptoms, or dental pain. She has had 6 weeks of bilateral shoulder and hip girdle aching and morning stiffness lasting over an hour, consistent with possible polymyalgia rheumatica. No history of TB contact, no recent travel. Past medical history: hypertension, no diabetes. No chronic steroid use.
examination: Alert, mildly uncomfortable. Left temporal artery is thickened, tender to palpation, with reduced pulsation compared to the right. Scalp tenderness over the temporal region. No visual field defect on confrontation; pupils equal and reactive. Fundoscopy: optic discs appear normal, no pallor or oedema. No lymphadenopathy. Bilateral shoulder and hip girdle tenderness with preserved power. Cardiovascular and respiratory exam unremarkable. No focal neurological deficit.
imaging: Temporal artery duplex ultrasound: non-compressible 'halo' sign in the left temporal artery
citations: Harrison 22e - Giant Cell Arteritis and Polymyalgia Rheumatica
ACR/EULAR Recommendations for the Management of Giant Cell Arteritis 2021
contraindications: Avoid delaying corticosteroid therapy pending temporal artery biopsy if visual symptoms or high clinical suspicion - biopsy can remain positive for 1-2 weeks after starting steroids
Use caution with high-dose glucocorticoids in patients with poorly controlled diabetes, osteoporosis, or active infection - requires monitoring and bone protection
edgeCases: Jaw claudication and scalp tenderness are highly specific findings for GCA and should prompt urgent glucocorticoid initiation without waiting for biopsy
Concurrent polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms are present in up to 40-50% of GCA patients
Any visual symptoms (amaurosis fugax, diplopia, vision loss) constitute an ophthalmic emergency requiring immediate high-dose IV methylprednisolone
Normal ESR does not exclude GCA in a minority of cases; CRP is more sensitive
